# N-D Viewer Tutorial {#nd_viewer_tutorial}

This demo tours viewer.h's N-D pairwise-slice primitives on a plain 3D volume, a genuinely 4D one (3 space + 1 time), and a genuinely 5D one (3 space + time + channel), then embeds the actual interactive viewer for each right in this page (if you're reading the generated tutorial -- see docs/generate_tutorial.py) so you can click around them yourself. Output lands in: build/demo/nd_viewer/output

## Building a synthetic 3D volume

### Step 1
```cpp
Image<uint8_t,3> vol3d(data, {n,n,n})
```

A torus (donut shape), the classic axial/coronal/sagittal case viewer.h generalizes: DIM=3 has exactly C(3,2)=3 pairwise views, one per pair of the 3 spatial axes -- the same axial/coronal/sagittal triple a clinical volume viewer shows, just synchronized through pairwise_slice()'s one shared cursor instead of 3 separately-coded planes.

```text
vol3d.extent():   {40,40,40}
```

### Step 2
```cpp
embedNDViewer("3D torus", vol3d, "volume3d.ndlv")
```

In the generated tutorial page this becomes a live grid of all 3 pairwise views -- click or drag in any panel to move the shared cursor and watch the other two panels jump to match, exactly the clinical triple-view interaction, generalized.

```text
3D torus: volume3d.ndlv
```

## Building a synthetic 4D (space x time) volume

### Step 3
```cpp
Image<uint8_t,4> vol(data, {n,n,n,nt})
```

A sphere whose center drifts diagonally and whose radius pulses sinusoidally over a 4th (time) axis -- deliberately not a static 3D shape just repeated across time, so the views involving the time axis show something genuinely different from the 3 purely- spatial ones below.

```text
extent:   {28,28,28,16}
```

## Checking one pairwise slice by hand

### Step 4
```cpp
auto slice03 = pairwise_slice<0,3>(vol, cursor);   // space axis 0 vs. time
```

pairwise_slice<AxisA,AxisB>() extracts the zero-copy 2D view spanning two axes, fixed elsewhere at cursor -- here axis 0 (an X position) against axis 3 (time), fixed at the volume's spatial center along Y/Z. Since the sphere's radius pulses over time, this slice should show a wavy band (wide where the pulsing sphere is large at this X position, narrow or absent where it's small), not a straight bar -- exactly the "space vs. time trace" pairwise_slice() makes viewable at all, generalizing the classic axial/coronal/sagittal synchronized 3-plane viewer to a 4th (or Nth) axis that isn't spatial at all.

```text
slice03.extent():   {28,16}  (expected {28,16})
```

## Embedding the interactive viewer

### Step 5
```cpp
VoxelSpacing<4> spacing;   // 3 spatial axes in mm, the time axis in s
```

viewer.h's VoxelSpacing<DIM> is optional per-axis physical calibration -- deliberately not part of Image itself (see VoxelSpacing's own comment for why), so it's supplied separately, right where it's actually used. Axes 0-2 (space) share one unit ("mm"), axis 3 (time) uses a different one ("s") entirely -- this is exactly the case a single shared physical scale can't handle: 2.0mm x 28 voxels is a 56mm cube, meaningfully compared between the 3 spatial axes, but there's no sane way to compare 56mm against 0.5s x 16 frames = 8s, so the two stay on separate physical scales (see ndlviewer.js's own computePerAxisPixelSizes() comment for how the viewer resolves that).

### Step 6
```cpp
embedNDViewer("4D sphere", vol, "volume.ndlv", &spacing)
```

Writes the whole 4D volume in ndlviewer.js's binary format, spacing included. In the generated tutorial page this becomes a live grid of all 6 pairwise views (space/space and space/time alike) -- click or drag in any panel to move the shared cursor and watch every other panel (including the ones showing the time axis) jump to match. Two visible effects of `spacing` specifically: the space/space panels are now perfect squares (all 3 spatial axes share "mm" at the same 2.0mm spacing, so their physical extents match exactly, unlike a voxel-count-only viewer that would already draw them square anyway since their voxel counts happen to match here too) -- but the space/time panels are visibly NOT square (56mm of physical space against 8s of physical time is not a 1:1 ratio), and hovering any panel now shows a second "physical (...)" line under the voxel line, in mm/s rather than raw indices.

```text
4D sphere (space x time): volume.ndlv
```

## Building a synthetic 5D (space x time x channel) volume

### Step 7
```cpp
Image<uint8_t,5> vol5d(data, {n,n,n,nt,nc})
```

A sphere whose center drifts over a time axis (axis 3) and whose radius pulses over a 5th "channel" axis (axis 4) at a different phase -- so axes 3 and 4 aren't just two copies of the same signal: the (3,4) pairwise view traces a genuinely 2D Lissajous-style curve, not a straight diagonal, and this is the first example where none of the C(5,2)=10 pairwise views are a disguised lower-DIM case.

```text
extent:   {20,20,20,10,8}
```

### Step 8
```cpp
embedNDViewer("5D sphere", vol5d, "volume5d.ndlv")
```

Writes the whole 5D volume in ndlviewer.js's binary format. In the generated tutorial page this becomes a live grid of all 10 pairwise views: 3 purely spatial (0-1, 0-2, 1-2), 6 mixing one spatial axis with time or channel, and the 1 pure time-vs-channel view (3-4) where the Lissajous curve is most visible. Same viewer code as the 3D and 4D examples above, still nothing special-cased about DIM.

```text
5D sphere (space x time x channel): volume5d.ndlv
```

All output written to: build/demo/nd_viewer/output If you're viewing the generated tutorial page, scroll up to the three embedded viewers: the 3D torus's 3 panels are the classic synchronized axial/coronal/sagittal triple; the 4D sphere's top-left 3 panels (axes 0-1, 0-2, 1-2) are the same kind of synchronized space/space views, while its other 3 (0-3, 1-3, 2-3) plot space against time, so dragging the time axis's own crosshair scrubs through the sphere's drift and pulse directly; the 5D sphere adds a channel axis on top of that, so its (3,4) panel is the one pure time-vs-channel view. Same viewer code, same pairwise_slice() primitive, DIM=3 through DIM=5 alike -- nothing about it is special-cased to any particular dimension count.
